The `tofu plan` command creates an execution plan, which lets you preview the changes that OpenTofu plans to make to your infrastructure.
developers can use speculative plans to verify the effect of their changes before submitting them for code review
Destroy mode: creates a plan whose goal is to destroy all remote objects that currently exist, leaving an empty OpenTofu state.
Refresh-only mode: creates a plan whose goal is only to update the OpenTofu state and any root module output values to match changes made to remote objects outside of OpenTofu.

The `tofu test` command lets you test your OpenTofu configuration by creating real infrastructure and checking that the required conditions (assertions) are met. Once the test is complete, OpenTofu destroys the resources it created.
The `tofu import` command imports existing resources into OpenTofu.

Update all your modules programmatically with a single variable change. Never miss updating a module version by accident - keep your infrastructure consistent and secure with centralized version management.
OpenTofu builds a graph of all your resources, and parallelizes the creation and modification of any non-dependent resources.

One commenter really liked the new name and branding: cohesive, easy to pronounce, with a good-looking website.

Neither the GitHub page nor the official website made clear what OpenTofu actually is or does. It repeatedly says it's a fork, so the user had to open the website of the original product to understand it.
Website feedback: the landing page lacks a 'Getting Started' section, and the license info is easy to find in the GitHub repo but not visible on the website.

Called the name 'Tofu' a poor choice: searching for it is going to be a terrible time, and they wondered how confused ChatGPT-style tools would get. They said they were more motivated to leave HCL/TF entirely for a CUE-based approach.
A consultant said the name is cute but won't help convince technology leaders to adopt the project over Terraform.
Asked whether OpenTofu plans to maintain the Terraform language server (terraform-ls), noting they couldn't find any language-server repository in the project.
"Fortunately using OpenTofu is just s/terraform/opentofu/g at this point."

A 5-year heavy Terraform user complained about Terraform's obtuse interface, such as iterating nested maps, and maintainers refusing requested features like dynamic provider blocks as 'not possible'. They said OpenTofu is already tackling many of their gripes and feature requests, and doing so eagerly.
Reading the description 'OpenTofu is a Terraform fork...', a commenter said they still had no idea what it is. They dislike product descriptions of the form 'X is like Y'.

A consultancy reported that OpenTofu is an easy migration. They moved one client, started a new client project on tofu, and were beginning to migrate another client, saying community opinion is shifting in OpenTofu's favor.

Commenter said OpenTofu has proven well-run enough to ship a new release with both Terraform compatibility and OpenTofu-specific enhancements, making it a no-brainer for Oracle versus paying for a Terraform resale license.

Seeing a for_each implementation for import blocks, a user said they were 'officially on board with this project', having been told for years this was impossible. They later realized they may have confused it with provider blocks and pleaded for for_each on providers too.

On OpenTofu 1.7, a user said provider-defined functions make them nervous as another tool for creating impure monstrosities. They were very excited about state encryption, though they wondered if an encrypted state file is safe to commit to a public repo.
"OpenTofu is already diverging from upstream but is relying on upstream providers so I'm not sure how to feel about it."

Critic said OpenTofu looks like 'the same old thing with a different owner'. They argued maintainers act like they own it and don't care about users, and that it's mainly a hedge for SaaS vendors wanting a permissive license rather than a community effort.

A user worried that OpenTofu adding features Terraform won't understand could fracture or bifurcate the ecosystem, creating extra work for module authors. They felt no urgency to migrate just because HashiCorp changed its license, calling it more of a group policy for affected SaaS vendors.
